topics.title: Is this normal?
topics.intro: Answers from AAC research and speech-language practice. Every child is different: your SLP knows yours best.

answers.q: What do I need?
answers.a: An iPad, or any device with a modern browser. Tap Create your child's board. That's it.

answers.q: Where do I start?
answers.a:
Three things make the first week work.

Add the people they call for, with names and photos.

Pick two or three words you'll use today (more, go, help) and show them with Spotlight.

Then model: point to words on their board while you talk, and let them explore without being tested.

answers.q: Do I need an account to start?
answers.a: No. Build the board first. When you've added your own people, save it with your email so it's backed up.

answers.q: How do I put Pip on the home screen like an app?
answers.a:
On an iPad or iPhone: open Pip in Safari, tap the Share button, then Add to Home Screen. On Android: open the browser menu and tap Install app or Add to Home screen.

Pip then opens full screen from its own icon and keeps working without the internet.

answers.q: Can I see the tour again?
answers.a: Yes. Settings, Overview, Replay the tour.

answers.q: Is Pip for teens and adults?
answers.a: Yes. Choose "a teen or adult" when you start, and you can choose words-only buttons.

answers.q: Can I bring my board over from another app?
answers.a: Pip is built differently, so you'll set up fresh, but it's quick, and many families run Pip alongside their old app while they switch.

answers.q: They press the same button over and over, or tap at random. Is that OK?
answers.a:
Yes, and it's a good sign. It's called AAC babbling. Like a baby saying "ba-ba-ba", they're learning where each word lives and what it sounds like.

Answer as if they meant it ("More? You want more!"), and now and then show the next word ("more… juice"). Please don't turn the sound off or put Pip away. That's like covering a talking child's mouth.

answers.q: They won't use Pip yet. Are we doing something wrong?
answers.a:
No. That's expected at first. Children hear thousands of words before they say one, and AAC is learned the same way: by watching you use it.

Point to words on their board as you talk ("we GO outside"), without asking them to copy you. Keep Pip in reach all day. Weeks or months before the first words of their own is normal.

answers.q: How do I teach them to use it?
answers.a:
Show, don't test. This is called modeling. Point to the words on their board while you say them, in real moments: snack, bath, play, the car.

Use one more word than they do. If they say "go", you show "go outside". Then wait: count to five in your head and give them a turn. Don't make them repeat a word, or tap it to get something.

Spotlight lights up the words you're teaching, so they're easy to find for both of you.

answers.q: Will Pip stop them from learning to talk?
answers.a:
No. Decades of research show AAC doesn't hold back speech, and many children say more out loud once they have a reliable way to be understood.

If they start saying words, celebrate it, and keep Pip there for when speech is hard.

answers.q: Are they ready for AAC? Are they too young?
answers.a: There's nothing to get ready for. Speech-language experts agree there are no prerequisites for AAC: not age, not attention span, not understanding pictures. Children learn it by using it, and toddlers can start too.

answers.q: They can say some words. Do they still need AAC?
answers.a: Often, yes. Many children who say some words use AAC for longer sentences, for words that are hard to say, when they're tired or upset, or with people who don't know them well. Using both is common, and both count.

answers.q: They say silly or rude words, or "no" all the time.
answers.a:
That's communication, and it's a big step: they've found out their words make things happen.

Answer like you would a talking child. Laugh at the joke, or say "You're mad. You can say stop." Saying no matters too. Never take Pip away as a punishment. It's their voice.

answers.q: Should I put Pip away when they misbehave, or at bedtime?
answers.a:
Keep it within reach all day: meals, the car, the park, bedtime. A child can't learn words they can't reach, and can't tell you what's wrong without them.

Pip isn't screen time. There are no games or videos. It's how they talk.

answers.q: They tap buttons to calm down or just to hear the sounds (stimming).
answers.a:
Many children do. Repeating sounds can be soothing, and it's often learning at the same time.

If it gets in the way, give it a time and place rather than taking Pip away. Your SLP can help you tell which it is.

answers.q: They use Pip at home but not at school (or the other way round).
answers.a:
Very common. New places and new people take time.

Invite the teacher as a helper so they see the same words, and ask them to model on the board during class. A short Spotlight list for school routines (help, all done, bathroom, my turn) gives everyone the same few words to show.

answers.q: They talk out loud more now and use Pip less.
answers.a: That's a win. Keep Pip nearby for the times speech is hard: when they're tired, upset, somewhere loud, or with new people. Many people use both for years.

answers.q: How long until they use it? Progress feels slow.
answers.a:
Every child's pace is different, and weeks or months is normal. Look for small wins: a word said on their own, a word you modeled tapped back, a new word.

Settings, Progress counts these from their own taps, so you can see change you might miss day to day.

answers.q: Why are the buttons little words like "go" and "more" instead of things like "apple"?
answers.a:
Because a few hundred small words make up most of what all of us say. "More", "go", "stop", "help", "not", "like" work everywhere, all day, and they never move. That's why they're on the main board.

The things they love belong on Pip too: add their people, foods and toys.

answers.q: They get upset when I touch their board.
answers.a:
Some children feel the board is theirs, and that's fair. Ask first ("Can I show you?").

Or model from your own phone: link it in Team & devices, then turn on Model from this device on its Spotlight page. Words you tap there light up on their board, and they never lose hold of it.

answers.q: How do I add a new word?
answers.a:
Settings, Overview, Add a word. Type the word and Pip finds a picture for it. You can use your own photo instead, or record your own voice for it.

With Pip Lifetime (and during the free week), a word you type also speaks in the board's voice.

answers.q: How do I add family names and photos?
answers.a: Settings, Words, Names, photos, and places. Add the people they call for and the places Pip should suggest. Real photos of real people work best.

answers.q: What do the sentence buttons do? (✨ Fix it, ❓ Question, ⏪ Past, ⏩ Future)
answers.a:
They turn the words your child tapped into a spoken sentence, without adding ideas.

✨ Fix it (the wand) adds the small words: "me hungry" becomes "I am hungry." ❓ Question asks it: "more" becomes "More?" ⏪ Past says it in the past tense: "go park" becomes "Went to the park." ⏩ Future says it in the future: "go park" becomes "Going to the park."

They never add a want, a person, or an idea your child didn't tap. They need the internet and Pip Lifetime. You can hide any of them in Settings, Talking.

answers.q: Why does Pip say the sentence one word at a time instead of all together?
answers.a:
The natural sentence voice, the sentence buttons and the feeling faces need the internet and Pip Lifetime (or the free week). Without them Pip still says every word, one at a time, which can sound choppy. Nothing goes silent and nothing is taken away.

Check the Wi-Fi first. If it's on, see Get Pip Lifetime at the top of Settings.

answers.q: Can my child say things with feeling?
answers.a: Yes: happy, sad, or angry, for any sentence. Turn on Feeling faces in Settings, Talking. The faces sit at the end of the Smart bar; tap one and the sentence is said with that feeling.

answers.q: How do I change the voice?
answers.a: Settings, Talking, Change voice. Today there's Pip's own voice, Mia (younger, female), Leo (grown-up, male) and Sam (younger, male). Tap ▶ to hear each one say "I want an apple." A voice never changes the words, only how they sound. Choosing a voice is part of Pip Lifetime.

answers.q: Can Pip talk slower?
answers.a: Yes. Settings, Talking, Speaking speed: Slower, Normal or Faster. The voice keeps its pitch.

answers.q: How do I show them the words I'm teaching?
answers.a:
Use Spotlight. Pick today's words; they glow on the board and the rest dim, but every word still speaks. Point and say the glowing words as you go. It turns off by itself tonight.

Settings, Spotlight, Try it shows you how in a minute.

answers.q: What are the words in the bar above the board?
answers.a: That's the Smart bar. It suggests likely next words as your child builds a sentence, so they need fewer taps. The board itself never moves. You can also outline likely next words on the board in Settings, Language help.

answers.q: Why did a word change, like "want" to "wants"?
answers.a: That's Grammar help. After "he", the board shows "wants", "has", "him", so the sentence comes out right. Turn it off in Settings, Language help.

answers.q: Can they type words?
answers.a: Yes. Pip has a keyboard that keeps every letter in one place, in QWERTY or ABC order. Choose it in Settings, Board, Keyboard. Pick the letter order once: switching moves every letter.

answers.q: How do I see progress, or get a report for an IEP meeting?
answers.a: Settings, Progress. Every number comes from their own taps on this device: words, sentences, new words, by week, month or 90 days. Share report makes a PDF for an IEP meeting or your SLP. The full dashboard and report are part of Pip Lifetime.

answers.q: How do I stop them from changing the settings?
answers.a: Lock Settings with a PIN: Settings, Backup & privacy, Settings PIN. One PIN for everyone on this device. Pip never shows it, so a child watching can't learn it.

answers.q: I forgot the PIN.
answers.a: On the PIN screen, tap "Forgot the PIN?" and type "new pin". Then choose a new one.

answers.q: Can two people, like brothers and sisters, use the same iPad?
answers.a: Yes. Settings, Team & devices, Add a person. Each person keeps their own words, groups and backup. You can have Pip ask who's talking each time it opens.

answers.q: Does it work without Wi-Fi?
answers.a: Yes. Tapping a word and hearing it works with no internet. The natural sentence voice and the sentence buttons need the internet.

answers.q: Can I really change anything?
answers.a: Any word in any spot. Your photos, your names, your recordings. Show or hide groups. Start with 15 buttons or 90.

answers.q: Won't changing things confuse my child?
answers.a: Nothing changes unless you change it. Pip never moves, hides, or reshuffles words on its own, and when you do move one, Pip shows you first.

answers.q: Will the buttons move around?
answers.a: Never on their own. Suggestions live in a strip at the top; the board stays put.

answers.q: How do I make the buttons bigger?
answers.a: Settings, Board, Buttons per screen. Fewer buttons are bigger and easier to hit; more buttons reach a word in fewer taps. Pip shows you what moves before anything changes.

answers.q: What if my child outgrows the board?
answers.a: Grow from 15 to 30, 60, or 90 words without starting over.

answers.q: Can the buttons show words without pictures?
answers.a: Yes. Settings, Board, Buttons show: Words only. Every button keeps its place and color, and the word gets bigger.

answers.q: How do I hide or reorder groups?
answers.a: Settings, Words, Show groups. Drag to reorder; a hidden group keeps its words and its place. To add or rename a group, use Edit the board.

answers.q: Can I record my own voice for a word?
answers.a: Yes, for any word or name. Open the word (Settings, Words, All words) and tap Record your voice.

answers.q: How do grandparents and teachers join?
answers.a: Invite them as helpers on their own phones or laptops: Settings, Team & devices, Invite. Teachers, therapists and grandparents then see and edit the same board.

answers.q: What can a helper do?
answers.a: Helpers edit everything on the board from their own phone or laptop, and changes reach every linked device. An owner also invites and removes people and manages devices. Free includes one helper; Pip Lifetime adds everyone.

answers.q: How do I put the same board on another device?
answers.a: Settings, Team & devices, Add a device. It shows a code; type it on the other device. A linked device sees and edits everything for this person.

answers.q: Is Pip really free? What's the catch?
answers.a: Free means free. Your child taps a word and Pip says it, for as long as they need it. You also get 20 words of your own, one helper, backup, and Spotlight. Every new board starts with a free week of everything, including natural sentences and the sentence buttons. After that, keeping those costs $49 once. That's the whole catch.

answers.q: What does $49 get me?
answers.a: A natural voice that reads the whole sentence, the sentence buttons, feeling faces, a choice of voices, a voice for words you type, the full progress dashboard and report, unlimited words of your own, every helper on the team, every device, and 300 pictures drawn in Pip's style. Once. Forever.

answers.q: What happens when the free week ends?
answers.a: Nothing on the board is hidden or removed. Every word still speaks, one at a time. The natural sentence voice, the sentence buttons, feeling faces, a chosen voice and the full progress report wait for Pip Lifetime. Your words, helpers and devices stay as they are.

answers.q: Will you ever make it a subscription?
answers.a: No. A voice is not rented. Pip Lifetime is paid once, so there is nothing to renew or cancel.

answers.q: Is it $49 per child or per family?
answers.a: Per child: the person who speaks. Helpers never buy their own license.

answers.q: I have a code. Where do I type it?
answers.a: Settings, Get Pip Lifetime, Have a code? Type it and tap Use code.

answers.q: Can a grandparent or our SLP pay for it?
answers.a: Yes. Settings, Get Pip Lifetime, Copy unlock link. They open the link, pay, and Lifetime unlocks for your child.

answers.q: I'm an SLP. Do I pay?
answers.a: Never.

answers.q: Can our school buy it?
answers.a: Yes: license codes, 50% off 10 or more, purchase orders welcome.

answers.q: Why is it so much cheaper than the others?
answers.a: Because we price what it costs us, not what families have been forced to pay.

answers.q: What if the iPad breaks?
answers.a: Open Pip on any device and scan your child's card. Everything comes back.

answers.q: What is the recovery card?
answers.a: A page with a QR code that brings back every word, photo and setting if this device is lost or reset. Make it in Settings, Backup & privacy, print it, and keep it somewhere safe. Without it, a linked device, or a device backup, their words can't be recovered.

answers.q: What does Pip send off this device?
answers.a: As little as it can. To suggest next words and to make sentences, Pip sends the words in the sentence being built, with names hidden. Words you type are sent to the voice provider to speak them. Anonymous daily counts (how many words, how long the sentences) help us improve Pip; turn them off in Backup & privacy. Never a recording, a photo, or who you are.

answers.q: Does Pip listen to us?
answers.a: No. The microphone is only used when you choose to record a word.

answers.q: How do I delete our data?
answers.a: Settings, Backup & privacy, Delete from Pip. It's removed from sync after 30 days, and you can undo it any time before then. Only an owner can delete.

answers.q: Does Pip replace speech therapy?
answers.a: No. It makes therapy and home work together.
